what_its_for: Carfilzomib is a cancer medicine used to treat multiple myeloma, which is a type of blood cancer that affects plasma cells in your bone marrow. It is usually given when other treatments have not worked or have stopped working. It works by blocking certain proteins inside cancer cells that help them grow and survive, causing the cancer cells to die.
how_to_take: Carfilzomib is NOT a pill you take at home. It is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor at a clinic or hospital. Each infusion takes about 10 to 30 minutes. You will need to drink plenty of fluids (water) before and after each dose to help protect your kidneys. Your care team will also give you other medicines before the infusion, such as fluids through your IV and a steroid called dexamethasone, to help prevent side effects.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the exact dose based on your body size (height and weight). Carfilzomib is usually given on specific days each week, in cycles that are typically 28 days long. A common schedule is to receive it on Days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15, and 16 of each 28-day cycle, followed by a rest period. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how you respond to treatment or if you have side effects. Never try to change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because carfilzomib is given at a clinic by a healthcare professional, it is very important to keep all your scheduled appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do not try to 'double up' or make up a missed dose on your own. Your care team will decide the best way to get your treatment back on track.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. If you are ever given any supplies related to your treatment to take home, follow the specific storage instructions given to you by your pharmacist or nurse.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink plenty of water unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Avoid taking new prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal supplements without first asking your doctor or pharmacist, as some medicines can interact with carfilzomib. Avoid activities that could cause injury or bleeding, since this medicine can lower your platelet counts. Avoid crowds or people who are sick, as carfilzomib can weaken your immune system and make it harder for your body to fight infections. Women of childbearing age should use effective birth control during treatment and for a period of time afterward, as carfilzomib can harm an unborn baby. Men should also use contraception during treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: chest pain, shortness of breath, or trouble breathing (signs of heart or lung problems); swelling of your legs, feet, or ankles; sudden severe headache, confusion, vision changes, or seizures; signs of infection such as fever (temperature above 100.4°F or 38°C), chills, or sore throat; unusual bleeding or bruising; severe tiredness or dizziness; little or no urination, or swelling that could signal kidney problems; severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; pain, redness, or sores in your mouth. These symptoms could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: It may take several cycles of treatment before you or your doctor can tell if carfilzomib is working. Your doctor will regularly monitor your condition with blood tests and other evaluations. Some patients begin to see improvements within the first few cycles, while others may take longer. Keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can track your progress. Do not stop treatment on your own even if you feel well or feel worse — always talk to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, especially heart, kidney, and breathing problems. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, as carfilzomib can affect kidney function. Your team will check your kidney health regularly. Heart problems: Tell your doctor if you have a history of heart disease, high blood pressure, or heart failure, as carfilzomib can cause heart-related side effects. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Carfilzomib can harm an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Women should not breastfeed while receiving this treatment. Both men and women should use reliable contraception during treatment and for some time after the last dose — ask your doctor how long. Children: Carfilzomib has not been studied in children and is not approved for use in patients under 18 years of age.
